1:
Calvin opens by settling what the poem laments. The prophet, following the alphabet a fourth time, deplores the ruin of the city and the destruction of the priesthood and the kingdom; and those are mistaken, he says, who take it for a lament over the death of a king, since much in it does not suit that event, the enemy not having reached the city then nor the stones of the Temple been cast into the streets. He notes that the chapter opens with the same exclamation as the first two, and that the verbs stand in the future used for the present. Ellicott compares the structure likewise, that the poem reproduces the character of the earlier two but traces more fully the connection between the sufferings and the sins.

What the gold and the holy stones stand for is the first real division. Henry takes them of the temple: the gold with which it was overlaid was smoked and sullied when the house was burned, thrown among the rubbish and converted to common uses, while the wrought stones of the sanctuary lay mingled without distinction among the common ruins; and when the God of the sanctuary was provoked to withdraw, no wonder the stones of it were profaned. Ellicott takes them for material treasures of palace or temple and nothing more, and argues from the repetition of the phrase about the top of every street, used earlier of children, that the words cover all that was most precious in the city. Clarke allows the temple but presses further, that the words apply particularly to the fallen priests and apostate prophets, the holy stones being the godly men who were even then the living stones of which God built his Church. He also works the metal itself: native gold from the mine has become tarnished contrary to its nature, and even the stamped gold that made it current is adulterated past passing. Gill glosses the dimming as a covering, the gold hid with rust or dust so that it can scarcely be discerned; Wesley notes the scattering in every street.

Who the precious sons are divides them again. Gill takes them for all the sons of Zion, rejecting the Jewish interpreters who make them a king and his children; Zion is the church, and her sons are her spiritual seed, precious not in themselves, being of the fallen race of Adam, nor in their own esteem or that of the world, but in the eye of God. Ellicott likewise refuses to confine the word to a class, whether priests or nobles, and applies it to all the sons of Zion in their ideal character as a kingdom of priests. Calvin restricts it to the chief men and the counsellors of the king, now stripped of all dignity; Wesley names nobles, priests and good men, and Clarke the priests and believers, once of the pure standard of holiness and now vessels of dishonour.

Two notes attach to the figure of the pitcher. Ellicott presses the verb, literally to be weighed with, so that the sons had been equal to their weight in fine gold, the work of God, and are now the work of the potter. Calvin sees an allusion to an earlier prophecy of the same writer, who went into the house of the potter and saw a vessel remodelled when it did not please him, the people being clay in the hand of God; and he adds that the description of ruin was written to remind a people who had scoffed at every threatening that what was predicted had been fulfilled. Keil and Delitzsch mark the order of the examples that follow, beginning with children, ascending to adults and ending with princes, and note that the misery is set out by comparing wild animals toward their young with the mothers of the city, since even jackals give the breast.
3:
What creature is meant divides the voices three ways. Gill reports dragons and seals before settling on whales, and marshals his authorities: Bochart has proved from various writers that they have breasts and milk, though the paps are hidden as in cases and must be drawn out, which is what Jarchi observed of a covering they uncover; and he cites the ancients for the dolphin and the sea calf suckling their young. Clarke agrees on whales but widens the word to all large and cruel creatures, aquatic or terrestrial; he adds a curious rendering from an old manuscript Bible of his own. Ellicott rejects both and gives jackals, noting that the same word is elsewhere rendered dragons and that jackals are combined with ostriches elsewhere as here. Calvin makes them serpents, and objects to the received construction on grammatical grounds: many take the daughter of the people to be the one called cruel, but the one word is feminine and the other masculine, so the sense must be that the whelps of serpents are better used than this people, since serpents, void as they are of humanity, still nourish their brood and give them the breast. He dismisses as a figment the Jewish claim that the breasts of serpents are covered with scales, and takes the drawing out for a common phrase from common practice, since a woman draws out the breast when she gives suck.

The ostrich needs no dispute. Wesley has the mothers become cruel, or forced to appear so, having through the famine no milk to give and nothing to relieve their children, like ostriches that lay their eggs and leave them in the sand; Ellicott notes that a like reference to the want of maternal instinct in that bird is found elsewhere.

The children and then the adults are set out in order. Gill takes the cleaving tongue as want of the milk that is both food and drink to an infant, and Keil and Delitzsch note that the second clause passes from sucklings to little children. Calvin observes the same step, that the latter clause speaks not of sucklings but of children three or four years old, and presses the unnaturalness of the first, since mothers would pour out their own blood to feed their infants, so that a tongue cleaving to the palate seemed beyond nature; he also corrects the tense, the verbs being past and not present as in our version. Keil and Delitzsch add a note on a phrase variously rendered because the verb is construed nowhere else with that preposition; they reject the Aramaic sign of the object and the rendering after their heart is desire, preferring the sense of nibbling round something.

The reversal for the great is described alike by all. Gill has those brought up in the palace or in the houses of noblemen, used to fare sumptuously, now wandering the streets seeking food, the Latin version making them perish in the ways. Ellicott renders the second clause literally as those that were carried, and takes the scarlet for the shawls of the rich dyed in purple, so that those once wrapped in them now threw themselves on dunghills as their only refuge. Clarke has them lie on straw or rubbish instead of the costly carpets they formerly stretched themselves on, and Calvin explains that the dunghills were heaps gathered for fuel instead of wood; the embracing seems hyperbolical, he grants, but ought not to appear incredible given what he has already had to narrate. On the verse that follows, Keil and Delitzsch dissent from most expositors, who take the two words for iniquity and sin in the sense of punishment: that meaning, they say, has not been established, since the words mean offence and sin, sometimes including their consequences, but nowhere castigation, and the scholar who argues that the context demands punishment has omitted a consecutive particle.
6:
Whether the verse speaks of guilt or of penalty is argued at length. Calvin allows both, each word being able to mean sin or its punishment, and grants that a useful doctrine follows from the first sense, that we may judge the grievousness of our sins by the greatness of our punishment, since God never exceeds what is just, other prophets having already charged this people with equalling and surpassing Sodom. But because the verse dwells only on the grievousness of the suffering he takes punishment to be meant, saying that he regards not what is plausible but what is true. Ellicott holds the opposite, that both words point to guilt rather than its penalty, though the greatness of the guilt is inferred from the greatness of the suffering. Clarke and Wesley weigh the two ruins: one city was destroyed in a moment while her inhabitants were in health, the other fell by lingering calamities, some by the sword and some by famine. On the clause about hands, Ellicott renders it literally that none went round about her, meaning the destruction was the direct work of God and not of human agents with their more merciless tortures; Clarke reports a rendering that hands were not weakened in her.

The next word divides them four to two. Clarke denies that it always means a man separated under a vow, says it sometimes denotes what is chief or eminent, and adopts a rendering that gives her nobles. Keil and Delitzsch agree, taking the word for princes, separated here not by vow but by dignity. Wesley makes them her separated ones, distinguished by birth, estate or place of magistracy; Gill reports the same view, that they were sons of nobles, since the word carries the sense of a crown, noting that Jarchi mentions this reading and rejects it while many receive it. Ellicott defends the traditional rendering: there is no reason to abandon it, since another prophet shows the Nazarites were prominent during the monarchy, and this writer, as his admiration of the Rechabites shows, was likely to think of them with reverence, their temperance making them conspicuous for an almost angelic beauty. Calvin agrees, taking them for men not content with the common observance of the Law who consecrated themselves for a season, and adds that since a man abstaining from wine is apt to grow pale, their ruddiness is the more remarkable.

What the colours describe is disputed too. Clarke refers the first line to the whiteness of the skin and the second to the flesh, and takes the sapphire for the veins, since the verb means to intersect as the blue veins do on the body. Keil and Delitzsch reject a scholar who referred the whiteness to clothing because easterners have not milk-white faces, since the second clause plainly speaks of bodily form. Ellicott agrees that the red and white complexion was the eastern ideal of comeliness, would render the last word not polishing but their form, and for rubies reads coral. Calvin takes the sapphire for smoothness, which he supports from the contrast at the end of the following verse, where the skin has become like a dried stick whose rind is shrivelled.

The reversal is stated in a single stroke. Gill has those who looked as pure as snow and as clear as pearls now black as charcoal, or, as he would render it, darker than blackness itself. Ellicott sets the two pictures side by side, the bloom and beauty of health against the wan and spectral looks of starvation. Calvin adds that they were so deformed as not to be known even in the open street; and he floats a possibility about the word for blackness, that since a river is called by that name for its muddy waters, the line might read that their appearance became darker than the river.
9:
The comparison of the two deaths is explained differently. Gill is careful that the better touches not their state after death but their manner of dying, since those cut down by the sword felt less pain than those who perished by famine and died as it were by inches. Calvin says sudden death is the easiest, and recalls the complaint elsewhere that the ungodly are taken away in a moment while the faithful protract life in languor; yet a violent death is always horrible, since a man who dies on his bed yields to his fate while one slain by the sword is snatched away contrary to nature, so the comparison only amplifies the atrocity of the punishment. The clause that follows is difficult. Ellicott notes that the italics of the English mark the trouble, the words standing literally as from the fruits of the field, and reports a reading that refers them to men struck down while fruits were still to be had; but he holds the construction of a psalm sufficient to support the received version. Calvin likewise reports a reading that supplies a defect, and prefers a more emphatic sense, that the productions of the earth, the servant of the bounty of God, took vengeance by refusing their usual supply.

On the mothers all four converge on one word. Gill notes that these were women naturally tenderhearted to their offspring, made cruel only by the soreness of the famine. Keil and Delitzsch say the predicate compassionate, applied to hands, makes the contrast with the innate love of mothers particularly prominent. Clarke presses it further, that the thing was done not by mothers cruel and brutal but by the tender-hearted, and adds that from such scenes it is well to pass with as hasty a step as possible. Calvin explains why the word is used at all: it is not praise, and no one is to think the mothers had kept their natural feeling; the point is that women who would otherwise have been humane were seized with a madness that came upon them from the vengeance of God.

The completeness of the wrath marks finality. Calvin says nothing was wanting to the extreme vengeance, for chastised in an ordinary way they would have extenuated their sins as before; God is content with moderate punishment provided men be roused, but when he pours out his wrath there is no hope of repentance, and vengeance overflowing like a deluge is a sign of final despair. He presses the word foundations, since fire commonly takes the roofs and very rarely penetrates so deep; the destruction meant left nothing remaining, for where ruins are left there is at least an intimation of a future restoration. Keil and Delitzsch say the same without the figure, the fire kindled in Zion being not the actual burning only but a symbol of complete destruction by the wrath of God, and Ellicott that the phrase is partly literal, partly figurative.

Whether the last verse overstates the case is asked directly. Ellicott grants that, since the city had twice been taken before, the statement seems at first hyperbolical, but observes that after the second capture it was fortified by three kings and that the failure of Sennacherib had produced an impression that it was impregnable. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same verdict by another road, citing a scholar who explains the words from the strength of the city and from its defender, who had more than once delivered it wonderfully; the expression, they say, is overdrawn but cannot properly be called hyperbole. Clarke agrees that the place was so well fortified by nature and art that its capture appeared a miracle, and Calvin draws the conclusion the others leave implicit, that since the fortifications made all attempts seem vain, the taking of it cannot be ascribed to human forces but to a hidden power.
13:
The blame falls on the leaders, without excusing the led. Gill reports that Aben Ezra referred the words to the prophets of Baal and the priests of the high places, but holds the false prophets meant were those the people themselves had chosen; the people were not faultless, but these were the principals who led them into sin. Henry says the same: the people loved to have it so, and it was to please them that the prophets and priests did as they did, yet the fault is chiefly laid on those who should have taught them better, since the blood of the flock is required of the watchmen who gave no warning; and nothing ripens a people for ruin faster than the sins of their priests. Calvin explains why the charge comes only now: had the prophet begun by condemning the priests he would have found no credit, but once the ruin is shown to be a kind of prodigy the inference cannot be resisted. He too refuses to let the people shelter behind their teachers; the point is that their physicians had proved impostors, prophets and priests alike having been given to apply a remedy. Wesley states it as a rule, that ecclesiastical men were a great cause of both destructions of the city, and of most places that come to ruin.

The particular sin is persecution. Henry has the false prophets and corrupt priests join to shed the blood of the just, the blood of the prophets of God and of those who adhered to them; they shed not only the blood of their children, sacrificed to an idol, but the blood of righteous men, sacrificed to the crueller idol of enmity against the truth, and this was the sin the Lord would not pardon. Ellicott supplies the instances, a prophet stoned in the temple court, innocent blood shed by a king, and attempts on the life of the writer himself. Clarke says the same, that men persecuted the genuine prophets under pretence of zeal for religion and shed their blood openly in the city.

Who the blind are is disputed. Gill takes them for the prophets and priests, either literally, so that when the city fell they knew not which way to go, or spiritually, since for all their pretence to light they were blind leaders of the blind; Wesley likewise has them wander the streets polluting themselves with blood, so that a man could not touch one without being defiled, and there were so many that the streets could not be walked without touching some. Calvin refers the figure to the citizens at large: those who read only that the blind wandered and were polluted because filth lay everywhere do not reach the sense. His own reading is that a blind man cannot distinguish, and will touch a carcass or a diseased man unknowing; when pestilence is partial an unclean place can be avoided, but when no corner is without a corpse a man must pass on anyhow. Ellicott renders the verb literally as reeled, and takes the blindness for a lust of blood or hopeless despair, adding that the garments of the priests dripped so with blood that men shrank from touching them; Clarke would render the clause that they ran frantic through the streets and were stained with blood.

The following clause has resisted the commentators. Calvin says plainly that interpreters have not understood it: all give that they could not touch their garments, and since that rendering is obscure and almost absurd they explain it as a warning to avoid touching; but the prophet, he says, meant another thing. Keil and Delitzsch report a related dispute over the cry in the next verse, which many render as a shout raised about them rather than to them, since it was lepers who had to cry unclean, the warning going to the clean.
15:
Who cries, and to whom, is the first question. Gill has the people cry it to the priests, whom they abhorred and bade keep their distance, so that men who had cleansed others of leprosy were proclaimed unclean themselves; Ellicott the same, the warning the leper was bound to utter now coming from those he met, who start back in fear of defilement. Wesley reads it otherwise, that the Jews who made conscience of the law against touching dead bodies cried to the rest to leave the city, since it was so full of corpses that they could not stay without polluting themselves. Calvin keeps the cry general and finds an allusion he says has not been noticed, to the law which sent the leper away with rent garments and covered lips to cry unclean; the prophet uses the words metaphorically, that the city was infected as though lepers were everywhere and a man could not set foot outside his door without meeting uncleanness. On the flight, Clarke has the priests so bad that the heathen would not let them sojourn among them, Ellicott suspects the words refer to lost facts about murderers fleeing their countrymen and finding themselves abhorred abroad, and Calvin reads an allusion to the exile.

Whose voice speaks the next verse divides them. Gill says expressly that these are not the words of the heathen continued but of the prophet, the anger in the face of God having removed the people from their land and dispersed them. Wesley says the opposite, that the words seem to be the language of their enemies triumphing over them, who had no regard to the most venerable among them. Ellicott takes the face literally as the symbol of wrath and leaves the subject of the verbs to be supplied, whether enemies, heathen or men in general, who ceased to reverence the fugitive priests and elders; Keil and Delitzsch supply the enemy, take the face for the angry look, and add that the last word means not elders but old men, since it can only refer to the priests and prophets already spoken of.

Calvin raises a difficulty of his own. If God had promised through Moses that though dispersed to the four quarters of the world they would be gathered, and if the term of the exile was fixed beforehand, how can it be said that they were scattered from his face and would not be regarded again? His answer is that the prophet describes only what the eye could then see. The promise of return was certain, but anyone looking at the state of things could have hoped no such thing, the desolation being immense: no name left to the people, the priesthood extinguished, the royal dignity degraded, the city and the Temple overthrown.

The last verse turns to the reliance that invited the judgment. Gill has them look for the promised help until their eyes failed and they gave it up; Clarke names the allies as the Egyptians, who were neither able nor willing to help against the Chaldeans, and Ellicott the same, adding two renderings of his own, that the eyes still waste away looking for a vain help, and that the watching is better given as upon a watch-tower. Keil and Delitzsch place the emphasis on the opening word, whose form is abnormal, since it takes plural suffixes nowhere else and the ending is not found elsewhere as a noun suffix, so that it appears copied from the verb that follows. Calvin makes it a charge of sacrilege: to look for salvation from others rather than from God alone is to reduce him in a manner to nothing, since he demands no more than that we depend on him; and he observes that prosperity inebriates men, so that while they seem to themselves to stand they disregard God and seek help here and there.
18:
Who does the hunting is the first question. Calvin reports that many apply the verse to the Egyptians who enticed the people to flee to them, and grants they had been deceived by false promises; but he thinks the Chaldeans meant, who followed them as hunters, and corrects the tense, our version giving in the present what should be past. Keil and Delitzsch report the same dispute, noting that two scholars set aside as strange and fanciful the idea of a third that Egypt is still in view; and they give the drift of these verses as one argument: the people cling to their hopes and are nevertheless wholly in the power of the enemy, so that none can deceive himself once flight has failed and the king is taken. Gill and Clarke read the hunting off the siege works, the enemy shooting from their mounds at whoever walked the streets, so that men kept within doors; Ellicott would render it that they lie in wait, and takes the words for posts near the open places which people learned to avoid, the only cry possible then being that all was over.

Calvin sharpens it. Their enemies were like hunters, since they could not walk even through their own streets, having no liberty in the city itself, much less leave to range the fields. He takes the end at hand for final ruin, and the fulfilling of the days as a comparison with the life of a man, who fulfils his day when he leaves the world.

The eagles draw out the classical learning. Gill notes that they are the swiftest of birds to a proverb, cites a Roman writer who tells of a racer that dreamed he had become an eagle and was assured he would win, since no bird flies with such force, and reports the fiction that a god who wished to find the middle of the world sent two eagles of equal swiftness from east and west, which met at the spot. Ellicott would render pursuers rather than persecutors, and suggests that if the second clause refers to the flight of the king the mountains are the heights east of the city and the wilderness that of the valley below; Clarke has the people hunted like wild beasts by marauding parties while the main army lay before the city.

Who the anointed of the Lord is provokes the sharpest disagreement, two voices rejecting the same reading for the same reasons. Gill denies that it can be the earlier king whom the Targum and Jarchi name, since though he was the anointed he was slain and not taken, not taken in pits, not by these enemies but by others, and the kingdom did not cease with him; the last king of the line answers everything. Calvin calls the same application ignorant on the same grounds, that the earlier king fell in battle long before the city did, that the royal dignity continued after his death, and that the enemy never came to the city in his time. Calvin then presses a further point, that the last king, unlike as he was to his predecessor, was still of the posterity of David and so a type of Christ, and is called the anointed because his crown was not yet cast down. Clarke and Wesley agree without argument, Clarke adding that his eyes were put out so that he was unfit for any function of government. Ellicott turns from the person to the phrase, taking it for the breath of life and finding in it the ideal character of the king as the centre of the national life, as a Roman writer calls a ruler the vital spirit of his people; and he reads what follows as a scheme the capture rendered abortive, since those who followed the king had hoped to find refuge with a friendly neighbour.
21:
Henry sets the close of the poem against the rest. The psalms of lamentation commonly end with some word of comfort, which is as life from the dead and light shining out of darkness, and so does this one: the people are in distress, their prospects frightful, while their ill-natured neighbours insult over them. Two things are foretold for their encouragement, that an end shall be put to the troubles of the one and to the triumph of the other. On the first he is careful about the measure, that what is accomplished is not the fulness of punishment their iniquity deserved but of what God had designed, and what was needed to answer the end, the glorifying of his justice and the taking away of their sin; the troubles of his people, he adds, last no longer than till they have done the work they were sent to do. Ellicott reads the same turn as a vision of judgment that is also a vision of hope, the triumph of the neighbour having been the crowning sorrow of the mourner, and notes that the prophet returns to his favourite image of the cup.

Whether the call to rejoice is irony is disputed. Gill takes it so, citing Aben Ezra, that they are bidden go on with their mirth if they can since it will not last; Clarke calls it a strong irony and observes that having joined the conquerors they must share the desolations of the conquering city; Wesley says the joy shall be but for a little time, and takes the drunkenness for an intoxication that will make them naked; and Henry has them told to insult over the city until they have filled up the measure of their own iniquity. Calvin reports this as the common reading and dissents. He thinks the first clause states the summit of their misery rather than mocking the enemy, since nothing is harder to bear in wretchedness than the petulant insults of enemies, which wound more than all other evils; the consolation follows after, in the promise that these enemies would themselves be punished at last.

The closing promise divides the voices four ways. Gill divides the fulfilment between the seventy years and a later captivity, since some things in the chapter had their further accomplishment in the second destruction of the city. Clarke turns it forward to the Gospel: when the people receive Christ crucified they shall be gathered from all nations, one flock under one Shepherd, and carried no more into captivity. Ellicott takes the harder line, that read by later history the words belong among unfulfilled prophecies, since like all promises they depended on implied conditions, and the rejection of the Christ forfeited the blessing and made a prolonged chastisement necessary; yet for five centuries the words held good, and there was no thorough dispersion until the later conquest. Calvin reports the Jewish reading, that the verse must mean a much later dispersion, since otherwise the prediction does not accord with the event, the people having dwelt in Greece and Macedonia and the cities of Italy until an edict expelled them; he calls these refinements useless, holding that the prophet meant only that the punishment would need no repeating, since there was no call for a second exile when the whole land was already a solitude.

The last clause is read by its opposite. Clarke observes that when sin is pardoned it is said to be covered, so that a threat to uncover the sins of the enemy declares they will not be pardoned; Ellicott states the same rule. Wesley makes the two halves answer each other, that the one shall not be carried away for past sins while the other shall be visited by the punishment of hers.
